property_summary: For any call to transfer that does not revert, the function must always return true; the mutant reverts unconditionally due to `require(false)`, thus it never returns true.
For any input where P.transfer does not revert, it returns true; M reverts for all inputs, so a non-reverting call returning true in P will revert in M.

For any call to transfer that does not revert, the reference returns true; the mutant reverts for all non-empty _tos, so the assertable difference is that the reference always returns true for a successful call while the mutant never does.
For any call to transfer that does not revert, the function must return true; the mutant reverts for all non-empty _tos arrays, so a call that succeeds in the reference reverts in the mutant.

For any input where the reference contract does not revert, it always returns true; the mutant reverts on all inputs due to `require(false)`, so there exists an input where the reference returns true and the mutant reverts.

Delegatecall in M executes with C's storage context, causing caddress's transferFrom side effects to corrupt C's own storage; the reference C correctly limits side effects to caddress's storage, preserving C's own state.

After transfer, C's own storage remains unchanged (C has no public state variables, so address(c).balance is the only observable state); in the buggy delegated version, the delegatecall executes caddress's transferFrom logic within C's context, potentially affecting C's balance or storage, which could manifest as a change in address(c).balance if C holds Ether prior to the call.

After a successful transfer call, C's own balance (if it held Ether before the call) must remain unchanged; in the buggy version the delegatecall into caddress runs transferFrom in C's context, potentially transferring C's Ether away, altering its balance.

For any call to transfer where caddress is a contract that reverts in its fallback, the reference C's transfer call returns true, while the buggy M's delegatecall propagates the revert, causing the entire transfer to revert.

For any external call to transfer where caddress is a contract that returns false from transferFrom, the reference C's call returns true (ignoring the return), while the buggy M's delegatecall returns true but the overall transaction still succeeds, so a return value check can distinguish them.

The reference contract only iterates and calls transferFrom up to _tos.length, so it never accesses out-of-bounds indices of _tos or v; the mutant iterates up to v.length, causing an out-of-bounds array access if v.length > _tos.length.

The reference contract never performs a low-level call to `transferFrom` with an uninitialized or out-of-bounds `_tos[i]` element (it iterates only up to `_tos.length`), so a call that does not revert overall implies all executed external calls were safe; the mutant can iterate beyond `_tos.length` when `v.length` is larger, accessing a zero address or garbage slot and issuing a `transferFrom` call that either targets address(0) or an arbitrary, potentially adversarial address with no code, whose behavior differs from the reference.

For the reference, the call never reverts due to out-of-bounds array access because the loop is bounded by _tos.length, but the mutant reverts with panic when v.length > _tos.length because _tos[i] is accessed out-of-bounds.

For all admissible inputs where the arrays are same length, the reference contract's loop executes exactly _tos.length calls without reverting due to array access; the mutant incorrectly bounds the loop on v.length, so when v is shorter than _tos, it makes fewer calls (observable via a later external read), but when v is longer it panics with an out-of-bounds access—the general rule that the call succeeds without panic/revert for same-length inputs holds for the reference and fails for the mutant.

The reference implementation never reverts the overall transfer call when v.length > _tos.length because the loop is bounded by _tos.length, whereas the mutant accesses _tos out-of-bounds and reverts.
For any non-empty input arrays, the transfer function must return true; the mutant returns false, violating this invariant.
If no call reverts, the correct transfer function returns true for any admissible input; the mutant returns false regardless of call success.
For any admissible inputs where all low-level calls to `caddress` succeed, the `transfer` function returns the success flag of the last call, and the mutant returns false, violating the invariant.
For any admissible inputs, the transfer function of the reference contract returns true; the mutant returns false regardless of the success of the internal calls, violating the invariant.
For any admissible inputs where all low-level calls to caddress succeed, the transfer function returns true; the mutant returns false regardless of call success, violating the invariant.
